opus-5.5.text:
I think the key point is that uncertainty doesn't straightforwardly argue for caution in investment; it actually cuts the other way once you think about the shape of the payoff. If you take seriously even a modest probability that scaling compute and algorithms gets you to systems that can substitute for most human labor, the economic value at stake is enormous. Labor compensation is something like half of world GDP, on the order of tens of trillions of dollars a year. So even if you put, say, a 10 or 20 percent chance on getting there within a couple of decades, the expected value of being positioned for that outcome dwarfs the cost of the investments we're currently seeing, even the largest data center buildouts.

So from a purely economic, decision-theoretic standpoint, I'd say uncertainty should push you toward investing more than you would if you were confident it wouldn't happen, and the right amount is probably larger than what naive extrapolation of current revenues would justify. Current AI revenues are small relative to the potential, and if you anchor on them you'll underinvest relative to the option value.

That said, there are a few nuances. One is that investment isn't all-or-nothing. A lot of the value of scaling incrementally is informational: each new generation of models tells you something about how far the trend goes, whether capabilities keep improving with compute, and whether things like agency and long-horizon task performance are coming along. So a sensible strategy is to keep scaling while watching those signals closely, and be ready to ramp up much more aggressively if they look good, or pull back if returns clearly flatten.

Another is that the downside risk for any individual investor is real. Some companies will overbuild and lose a lot of money, much like in the railway or dot-com booms. But at the level of the economy as a whole, the asymmetry still favors substantial investment, because the cost of being too slow, if automation turns out to be feasible, is huge.

And finally, from a societal perspective, the same uncertainty means we should invest in understanding and preparing for that outcome too: the economic disruption, the safety questions, the governance challenges. If you think there's a meaningful chance labor automation happens, it would be strange to bet heavily on the technology while doing very little to prepare for the consequences.

r001.rationale: The response says the expected value of a chance of systems substituting for most human labor justifies investment. It does not clearly argue that partial labor automation itself can justify investment.

r002.rationale: The response identifies informational value from each scale-up: newer models can reveal how far the trend goes and whether capabilities continue improving, helping resolve uncertainty about labor automation's feasibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to notice is that the case for investing in scaling is actually quite robust to that uncertainty, and the reason is that the payoff is so asymmetric. If you think there's, say, a 10 or 20 percent chance that continued scaling gets you to systems that can do most of what human workers do, then the expected value of that is enormous, because the prize is essentially a large fraction of global output, which is on the order of a hundred trillion dollars a year. So even at fairly low probabilities, spending hundreds of billions, or even a few trillion, on compute and energy and chips looks reasonable in expectation. You don't need to be confident that it works for the investment to make sense.

Now, where the uncertainty really matters is in the shape of the investment rather than whether to invest. If you're uncertain about whether scaling gets you all the way, you want to be making bets that pay off in the intermediate worlds too. And I think that's actually what we're seeing. The models that exist today are already economically useful in software, in customer service, in some research tasks, and so the investment is partly justified by the near-term returns and partly by the option value on the bigger prize. That's a fairly healthy structure. The worry would be if the investment were only justified by the full-automation scenario, because then you'd have a lot of fragility if the timelines slip.

The other thing I'd say is that uncertainty cuts in both directions. People often frame it as, well, maybe this doesn't work, so we should be cautious about overbuilding. But there's also the scenario where it works faster than expected, and in that world, having underinvested in compute and energy infrastructure is extremely costly, because those have long lead times. You can't spin up gigawatts of power in a year. So if you take the uncertainty seriously, it actually argues for building more capacity than the median forecast would suggest, because the cost of being short in the good scenario is much larger than the cost of having excess capacity in the bad one.

I'd add one caveat, which is that this reasoning works at the level of society or the industry as a whole, but for an individual firm it's much trickier, because you need to capture the returns and not just generate them. A lot of the value from automation might flow to users or to whoever controls the complementary inputs, so a company can be right that scaling works and still lose money on it. But from the perspective of, is the world collectively investing too much or too little given the uncertainty, I'd still lean toward too little.

r001.rationale: The response says current models already have economic value in software, customer service, and research, so near-term returns help justify scaling even if full automation is uncertain.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty as affecting investment size and capacity, but does not identify reducing or resolving uncertainty about labor automation as an additional benefit of scale-ups.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish uncertainty about whether full labor automation is possible from uncertainty about how much economic value further scaling can produce. You don’t need to automate every job for AI to be enormously valuable. But you also shouldn’t take the value of automating all labor and treat that as the guaranteed payoff from building the next generation of models.

So I would think about investment in stages. You invest some amount, observe how capabilities improve, see whether those capabilities translate into useful products, and then update your expectations about the next investment. There’s value in learning whether the scaling trajectory is actually delivering what you hoped.

And uncertainty cuts both ways. It can justify caution, particularly when you’re committing to expensive infrastructure. But if there’s a meaningful probability of very large returns, substantial investment could still make sense. The important question is whether the investment looks attractive across a plausible range of outcomes, rather than only under the assumption that full labor automation arrives very soon.

r001.rationale: It says AI can be enormously valuable without automating every job and that investment may make sense despite uncertainty about full automation.

r002.rationale: It describes learning whether scaling improves capabilities and yields useful products, but does not identify resolving uncertainty about labor automation’s feasibility as an additional source of value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think uncertainty cuts both ways. If you’re uncertain about whether scaling will get us to full labor automation, that’s a reason to be cautious about assuming that any particular investment will pay off. But it isn’t necessarily a reason to invest less overall, because the payoff if it does work could be enormous.

You want to distinguish uncertainty about whether it’s possible from uncertainty about how much compute, data, and algorithmic progress it will require. In the second case, investing can also buy information. You train a more capable system, see where it succeeds and where it falls short, and update your expectations about the next investment.

So I’d favor a staged approach: make investments that let you learn, preserve the option to expand, and reassess as the evidence comes in. And I’d separate the private investment case from the social case. The prospect of automating labor might make scaling financially attractive, while still leaving important questions about safety and how the benefits are distributed.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a successful scaling investment could have an enormous payoff despite uncertainty, but it does not identify partial labor automation as a source of that expected value.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes learning how much compute, data, and algorithmic progress automation may require, but does not present resolving whether labor automation is feasible as an additional value from scale-ups.
